guide.1.example: Leave your fretting hand off the strings. Pluck the thickest string and say “E.” Let it ring for two counts. Continue A, D, G, B, E toward the thinnest string. Repeat once without looking at the names.
guide.1.listen: Six separate, ringing notes. The last E sounds higher than the first. Keep your picking hand clear of the string after each pluck.
guide.1.rescue: Work on just the thickest three strings: E, A, D. If a note stops abruptly, check that neither hand is touching the vibrating string.
guide.10.listen: The open A and thinnest E ring clearly. Each new chord begins on count 1, at the same slow pace.
guide.10.rescue: Work only on A. Pick its five strings separately. Reposition the ring fingertip if the thinnest E is silent. Practice A → D before adding E.
guide.11.listen: One clear note at a time, with equal gaps. Finish on A at low E fret 5 and notice the sense of arriving home.
guide.11.rescue: Use only low E frets 5 and 8, then A string fret 5. Play these three notes forward and backward before adding more of the pattern.
guide.12.listen: The notes follow the melody you hummed. Keep long notes long; do not speed up to get past a difficult change.
guide.12.rescue: Take only the first three notes in the tab. Hum them, find them, and play them slowly. Add one more note when those three feel familiar.
guide.13.listen: Similar volume and equal gaps between notes, including when you move to the next string.
guide.13.rescue: Use frets 1 and 2 on the B string only. Make two clear notes with relaxed fingers, then try those same frets on high E.
guide.14.listen: Only the two intended strings ring. G5 and A5 have the same shape, and the pulse stays even as the shape moves.
guide.14.rescue: Stay on G5: low E fret 3 and A fret 5. Pick the pair gently four times. Practice moving the shape silently before adding A5 strums.
guide.2.example: On the thinnest E string, put your index finger just behind fret 1, on the nut side of the wire. Pick once. Repeat at fret 2 with the middle finger, 3 with the ring finger, and 4 with the little finger. Start without a click, then try one note per beat at 50 BPM.
guide.2.listen: Four clear notes rising in pitch, with equal gaps. Use only enough pressure to stop the buzz; release the pressure between attempts.
guide.2.rescue: Use just frets 1 and 2. Move closer to the fret wire before adding pressure. Make the reach smaller and rest if the hand feels strained.
guide.3.example: Place your middle finger on string 5 (A), fret 2, and ring finger on string 4 (D), fret 2. Leave the other strings open. Pick all six separately, then strum downward on counts 1 and 3 while counting “1, 2, 3, 4.”
guide.3.listen: Every string rings, including the open G next to your ring finger. Two bars give you four evenly spaced strums.
guide.3.rescue: If the G is muted, curve your ring finger so its side clears that string. Recheck just A, D, and G before strumming again.
guide.4.example: Build G: middle finger on low E fret 3, index on A fret 2, ring on high E fret 3; D, G, and B stay open. Play Em for eight slow counts, then G for eight. Start with a single strum at the beginning of each group.
guide.4.listen: The new chord lands on count 1. Keep counting during the change, even when you need a silent beat to place the fingers.
guide.4.rescue: Practice the hand move without strumming. Place G, release, and rebuild it three times, then add Em at a slower pace.
guide.5.example: Build C: ring finger on A fret 3, middle on D fret 2, index on B fret 1. G and high E stay open. Pick from A toward high E, then strum those five strings. Alternate one C strum and one G strum, leaving four counts to change.
guide.5.listen: The open G and high E still ring. The lowest note of your C chord is the A string at fret 3; leave the thickest E out.
guide.5.rescue: Check the B string alone, then the open high E. Curve the index fingertip to clear high E. Practice starting the pick on A without changing chords.
guide.6.example: Build D: index on G fret 2, ring on B fret 3, middle on high E fret 2. Leave D open and strum only strings 4 through 1. Count four slow beats each on G, C, D, and G, strumming once at each chord change.
guide.6.listen: Four bright notes in D, with no low E or A. Keep the count moving through all four chords.
guide.6.rescue: Stay on D and pick its four strings separately. If high E is muted, check whether the ring finger is touching it. Add only C → D before the full loop.
guide.7.example: Play Em → G → C → D. Give each chord four counts and one down-strum on count 1. Repeat the loop twice. If that is comfortable, strum on counts 1 and 3. Make a short recording if you want to hear the changes back.
guide.7.listen: An even count from the first chord to the last. Notice which change takes longest; that is your next practice target.
guide.7.rescue: Choose only the slowest pair of chords. Give each eight counts. Practice the change three times, then return to the four-chord loop.
guide.8.listen: Five clear strings in Am; six in E major. The open thinnest E must ring in both shapes.
guide.8.rescue: Stay on Am. Check just B fret 1 and the open thinnest E. Curve the index fingertip so it does not silence the E. Add the change only after Am is clear.
guide.9.listen: The downstrokes stay on the numbers. The two upstrokes fit halfway between beats, without making the next downstroke late.
guide.9.rescue: Leave out the chord. Use muted strings and play only downstrokes on 1, 2, 3, 4. Add just the upstroke after 4, then the one after 2.
guide.phase.basics.listen: Clear starts, notes that ring for the intended length, and a relaxed hand. Compare one attempt with the next.
guide.phase.basics.rescue: Isolate one note or one hand movement. Remove the click until it is clear, then bring back a slow pulse.
guide.phase.chords.listen: Pick each intended string separately. Listen for missing notes, buzz, and changes that land late.
guide.phase.chords.rescue: Choose the hardest two shapes. Rehearse the change silently, check each string, then add one strum per chord.
guide.phase.lead.listen: A phrase with a clear start, space, and a deliberate ending. Compare any bend with its unbent target pitch.
guide.phase.lead.rescue: Take two or three notes from the phrase. Keep the rhythm and rests; leave out ornaments until the phrase is steady.
guide.phase.repertoire.listen: The transition into and out of the difficult section. Keep the pulse through a mistake and recover at the next phrase.
guide.phase.repertoire.rescue: Loop the last bar of the previous section and the first bar of the next. Join them slowly before adding the rest of the song.
guide.phase.rhythm.listen: Your count continues through rests. The next attack after a rest should line up with the pulse.
guide.phase.rhythm.rescue: Put down the guitar and clap the rhythm while counting. Add muted strings, then restore the pitches.
guide.phase.scales.listen: Even spaces between notes and a clear return to the root. Name the root before playing the pattern.
guide.phase.scales.rescue: Use the root and two nearby scale notes. Play them slowly in both directions before rebuilding the full pattern.
step.1.0.instruction: Rest the guitar comfortably. Leave the hand that presses the strings off the neck. Pluck the thickest string once. Its name is low E.
step.1.0.title: Find the thickest string
step.1.1.instruction: Move from the thickest string to the thinnest: E, A, D, G, B, E. Pluck one string at a time and say its name.
step.1.1.title: Name the six strings
step.1.2.instruction: Pluck each string again. Count “1, 2” before moving to the next. Keep both hands clear of the string while it rings.
step.1.2.title: Let each note ring
step.1.3.instruction: Look away from the string names. Say each name as you pluck from thickest to thinnest. If you forget, check the names and try again.
step.1.3.title: Try without looking
step.10.0.instruction: Place index on D fret 2, middle on G fret 2, and ring on B fret 2. Keep open A and the thinnest E clear. Leave out low E.
step.10.0.title: Build A major
step.10.1.instruction: Pick from A toward the thinnest E. Adjust the fingertips until each note rings. Then strum the five strings together.
step.10.1.title: Check all five strings
step.10.2.instruction: Play A → D → E → A. Give each chord four slow counts and strum once on count 1. Repeat twice.
step.10.2.title: Connect A, D, and E
step.10.3.instruction: Play A, then rebuild Am from lesson 8. Listen to the change in sound. The B string changes from fret 2 in A to fret 1 in Am.
step.10.3.title: Compare major and minor
step.11.0.instruction: Press the thickest E string at fret 5 and pick it. This note is A, the home note (root) of today’s scale.
step.11.0.title: Find the starting A
step.11.1.instruction: Play low E frets 5 then 8. Move to the A string and play frets 5 then 7. Use index at fret 5, ring at 7, and little finger at 8.
step.11.1.title: Start with two strings
step.11.2.instruction: Continue toward the thinnest string: D frets 5–7, G frets 5–7, B frets 5–8, high E frets 5–8. Play one note at a time. Use the map below if you lose your place.
step.11.2.title: Finish the pattern
step.11.3.instruction: Play the pattern backward until you reach low E fret 5. Pause on that A. First use equal, slow notes; try 60 BPM when the pattern feels familiar.
step.11.3.title: Return to the home note
step.12.0.instruction: Open Twinkle in the lesson materials below. Listen to the first short musical sentence, then hum it. You only need that small part for now.
step.12.0.title: Listen to one short part
step.12.1.instruction: Each line is a string; the top line is the thinnest string. A number tells you which fret to press. A 0 means play the string open.
step.12.1.title: Read the tab
step.12.2.instruction: Find the first few notes in the tab. Play them slowly until you can repeat them twice without stopping. Hum them again if you forget how they should sound.
step.12.2.title: Play the first phrase
step.12.3.instruction: Learn the next short part the same way. Join the two parts slowly. Continue one phrase at a time, keeping the same pace.
step.12.3.title: Add one phrase
step.13.0.instruction: Find the second-thinnest string, B. Play frets 1, 2, 3, 4 with index, middle, ring, and little finger, one note at a time.
step.13.0.title: Use the B string
step.13.1.instruction: Move to the thinnest E string and repeat frets 1, 2, 3, 4. Keep the gaps between notes equal.
step.13.1.title: Move to high E
step.13.2.instruction: Alternate those two strings. Keep unused fingertips near the strings without stiffening them. Release excess pressure after each note.
step.13.2.title: Keep movements small
step.13.3.instruction: Continue slowly for up to 60 seconds, keeping the notes at a similar volume. Take a break if the hand feels tired or strained.
step.13.3.title: Repeat comfortably
step.14.0.instruction: Play the thickest E string open and the A string at fret 2. Sound only those two strings. This is E5, a power chord.
step.14.0.title: Play two notes together
step.14.1.instruction: Place index on low E fret 3 and ring on A fret 5. Pick only those two strings together. Lightly touch unused strings to keep them quiet.
step.14.1.title: Move to G5
step.14.2.instruction: Slide both fingers two frets toward the guitar body: index to low E fret 5, ring to A fret 7. Keep the same two-string shape.
step.14.2.title: Move to A5
step.14.3.instruction: Count four beats per bar. Play G5 once per beat for two bars, then A5 once per beat for two bars. Repeat the whole pattern twice at a comfortable speed.
step.14.3.title: Make a four-bar pattern
step.2.0.instruction: Use the thinnest E string. Place your index fingertip just before the first metal fret wire, on the side nearer the tuning pegs. Pick the string once.
step.2.0.title: Place one fingertip
step.2.1.instruction: Slowly ease the pressure until the note buzzes. Add just enough pressure to make it clear again. Keep the fingertip close to the fret wire.
step.2.1.title: Find a light touch
step.2.2.instruction: Play fret 1 with index, fret 2 with middle, fret 3 with ring, and fret 4 with little finger. Play one note at a time on the same string.
step.2.2.title: Add the other fingers
step.2.3.instruction: Repeat 1–2–3–4 slowly with equal gaps. When that feels comfortable, use a metronome at 50 beats per minute, one note per click. Work toward the 60 BPM target later.
step.2.3.title: Give the notes equal time
step.3.0.instruction: Put your middle fingertip on the A string, fret 2. The A string is the second-thickest string.
step.3.0.title: Place the first finger
step.3.1.instruction: Put your ring fingertip on the D string, fret 2. D is the next string toward the floor. Leave the other four strings open: do not press them.
step.3.1.title: Place the second finger
step.3.2.instruction: Pick all six strings, thickest to thinnest. If one is silent or buzzy, adjust the nearby fingertip and pick that string again.
step.3.2.title: Check one string at a time
step.3.3.instruction: Count “1, 2, 3, 4” slowly. Brush down across all six strings on 1 and 3. Repeat the count four times for eight strums. This chord is E minor, written Em.
step.3.3.title: Play eight slow strums
step.4.0.instruction: Place middle finger on low E fret 3, index on A fret 2, and ring on the thinnest E fret 3. Leave D, G, and B open.
step.4.0.title: Build G
step.4.1.instruction: Pick each string separately, then strum all six together. Adjust any finger that touches a neighboring open string.
step.4.1.title: Check the sound
step.4.2.instruction: Play one Em strum. Count eight slow beats while moving to G. Strum G on the next count 1. Give yourself another eight counts to return to Em.
step.4.2.title: Change from Em to G
step.4.3.instruction: Repeat Em → G four times. Shorten the pause only when both chords ring clearly. Then try today’s target below.
step.4.3.title: Repeat the change
step.5.0.instruction: Place ring finger on A fret 3, middle on D fret 2, and index on B fret 1. Leave the G and thinnest E strings open.
step.5.0.title: Build C
step.5.1.instruction: Pick from the A string toward the thinnest E, one string at a time. Leave out the thickest E string. You should hear five notes.
step.5.1.title: Start on the A string
step.5.2.instruction: Keep the shape and brush down from A to the thinnest E. Repeat four times slowly. Check that your index finger leaves the thinnest E free to ring.
step.5.2.title: Strum five strings
step.5.3.instruction: Strum C once, count four slow beats, then strum G. Count four more beats and return to C. Repeat twice. Take more time to change if needed.
step.5.3.title: Connect C and G
step.6.0.instruction: Place index on G fret 2, ring on B fret 3, and middle on the thinnest E fret 2. The D string stays open.
step.6.0.title: Build D
step.6.1.instruction: Pick D, G, B, and the thinnest E separately. Then strum those four together. Leave out the thickest E and A strings.
step.6.1.title: Use only four strings
step.6.2.instruction: Strum C, then take four slow counts to form D. Strum D on the next count 1. Repeat the change three times.
step.6.2.title: Practice C to D
step.6.3.instruction: Play G → C → D → G. Give each chord four slow counts, with one strum on count 1. Start again after the last G.
step.6.3.title: Join G, C, and D
step.7.0.instruction: Count “1, 2, 3, 4” at a pace that gives you time to change chords. A metronome is optional at first.
step.7.0.title: Choose a comfortable speed
step.7.1.instruction: Play Em → G → C → D, with four counts per chord. Strum once on count 1. Repeat the loop twice.
step.7.1.title: Play the four chords
step.7.2.instruction: Choose the change that took longest. Practice just that pair three times. Give each chord eight counts if four feels rushed.
step.7.2.title: Fix one change
step.7.3.instruction: Return to the four-chord loop. Aim for two minutes at your comfortable pace. If you miss a chord, keep counting and join again on the next count 1.
step.7.3.title: Keep the music going
step.8.0.instruction: Place index on B fret 1, middle on D fret 2, and ring on G fret 2. Strum from the open A string toward the thinnest E. Leave out low E.
step.8.0.title: Build A minor
step.8.1.instruction: Move each finger one string toward the thickest string, keeping its fret: index to G fret 1, middle to A fret 2, ring to D fret 2. Strum all six strings.
step.8.1.title: Build E major
step.8.2.instruction: Pick every string of each chord separately. E major has a finger on G fret 1; E minor leaves that string open. Compare the sounds.
step.8.2.title: Hear the difference
step.8.3.instruction: Play eight slow strums on Am, then eight on E. Next, alternate one Am strum and one E strum, leaving four counts to change.
step.8.3.title: Change slowly
step.9.0.instruction: Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” evenly. The numbers are the main beats; “and” is halfway between them.
step.9.0.title: Say the count
step.9.1.instruction: Lightly touch the strings with your fretting hand so they do not ring. Strum down on each number and move up on each “and.”
step.9.1.title: Move the strumming hand
step.9.2.instruction: Keep that hand motion. Touch the strings on 1, 2, the “and” after 2, 3, 4, and the “and” after 4. Pass above the strings on the “and” after 1 and 3.
step.9.2.title: Leave two upstrokes silent
step.9.3.instruction: Hold G and play the same pattern. Repeat “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” eight times. Each full count is one bar. Slow down if you lose the count.
step.9.3.title: Add a G chord
term.bar.meaning: A group of beats. In 4/4, count 1, 2, 3, 4; that is one bar. Other time signatures group beats differently.
term.bpm.meaning: Beats per minute: the speed of the pulse. At 60 BPM, a metronome clicks once each second. Play one note per click unless the exercise says otherwise.
term.fret.meaning: The metal wires across the neck mark the frets. Fret 1 is nearest the tuning pegs. Press the string just before the wire, on the side nearer the pegs.
term.fretting-hand.meaning: The hand that presses the strings against the neck. Your other hand picks or strums.
term.muted.meaning: A string is kept from ringing, usually by touching it lightly. Muting can be intentional; a finger accidentally touching the next string can also silence it.
term.open-string.meaning: A string you play without pressing it against a fret.
term.pentatonic.meaning: A scale with five different note names. A minor pentatonic uses A, C, D, E, G. A box is one area of the neck where you can play those notes.
term.phrase.meaning: A short musical idea, like a sentence. Learn a few notes together, pause, then learn the next group.
term.power-chord.meaning: A chord made from a root and a fifth, sometimes with the root repeated higher. G5 means a G power chord; the 5 is not a fret number.
term.root.meaning: The note a chord or scale is named after. A is the root of A minor. Find it first so the pattern has a clear starting point.
term.string-numbers.meaning: String 1 is the thinnest E. String 6 is the thickest E. Thickest to thinnest: 6 E, 5 A, 4 D, 3 G, 2 B, 1 E.
term.strum.meaning: Brush across several strings in one motion. A downstroke moves from thicker strings toward thinner strings.
